page_1.audience: Deep-tech and infrastructure investors, AI hardware companies, data-center operators, and strategic thermal-management partners.
page_1.conveys:
1. This is a category change: thermal management becomes addressable and controllable rather than passive plumbing.
2. This has a credible entry point: the first product integrates with existing liquid-cooled AI hardware instead of requiring a new data center.
3. This can become a platform: the ceramic cell architecture creates defensible hardware, control data, and applications beyond AI racks.

page_2.elevator_pitch:
Vitriflux

A software-defined thermal backplane for AI hardware.

AI accelerators do not produce heat uniformly. Hotspots move across chips, boards, and racks as workloads change, but today’s cooling systems are fixed plumbing designed around a worst-case thermal map. Operators compensate with oversized pumps, aggressive coolant temperatures, redundant manifolds, and unused cooling capacity.

Vitriflux is developing a field-addressable ceramic plate that routes heat through hardware the way a network switch routes data. A grid of controllable thermal cells changes the preferred direction of heat flow in response to live temperature data, moving energy away from transient hotspots and toward whichever cooling interface has available capacity.

The initial product sits between accelerator modules and an existing liquid-cooling loop. It does not replace the facility cooling system or require changes to the processors. It adds an adaptive thermal-routing layer intended to increase rack density, reduce hotspot throttling, and let operators use installed cooling capacity more effectively.

Vitriflux begins with AI infrastructure, where every recovered watt and square centimeter has immediate value. The underlying platform could later extend to power electronics, battery systems, aerospace electronics, and industrial equipment with irregular thermal loads.

Problem solved: Static cooling architectures waste capacity and constrain compute density because they cannot respond spatially to changing heat loads.

anchor_writer_output.deck_generation_prompt:
This was the pitch people kept referring to afterward as the moment a familiar infrastructure problem suddenly looked like an unclaimed control layer. The founding team came across not as a startup trying to decorate a cooling component with software language, but as the rare synthesis group that could see the blind spot between materials science, thermal engineering, control systems, and AI infrastructure economics all at once. Their chemistry made the core claim feel less like a speculative analogy and more like an engineering inevitability waiting for the right people to articulate it: if compute has become dynamic, dense, and workload-shaped, then heat management cannot remain static, overprovisioned plumbing forever.

The team had the unmistakable profile of a problem-selected supergroup. The CEO had spent years close to advanced compute systems and knew how quickly thermal constraints become capital constraints once accelerators are packed at the edge of tolerable power density; this person spoke with the discipline of someone who had seen infrastructure buyers punish hand-waving and reward precise system-boundary thinking. The chief scientist was a field-crossing materials researcher whose reputation came from working at the edge of ceramic, ferroic, or interfacial transport phenomena and who was visibly more interested in first principles than hype; when this person described the cell-level hypothesis, the room understood that the mechanism was still under comparative evaluation, but also that the scientific reasoning was serious. The systems architect had previously built or operated high-reliability thermal, power, or hardware-control systems at scale and gave the company its practical spine: integration envelopes, control intervals, serviceability, connectors, manifold realities, fault behavior, deployment friction. The commercial operator had sold into hard technical organizations before and understood exactly how server OEMs, cooling providers, and infrastructure operators each read risk differently. And the team’s graphic designer and marketing lead was not an external polish layer but one of the essential translators of the company itself: someone with a background in technical brand systems for semiconductor, robotics, or industrial product launches, who understood how to make complex physical systems legible without softening them. This presentation was designed and produced by that person by hand, and every page carried their specific taste: graphite fields, ceramic blacks, copper pathing, thermal-vector overlays, terse engineering typography, and visual compositions that made the product feel simultaneously material and computational.

They were presenting into a room full of people who were unusually difficult to impress for different reasons. Deep-tech investors were alert to scientific overreach. AI hardware companies were prepared to dismiss anything that implied processor redesign or impossible packaging concessions. Data-center operators were primed to reject any idea that sounded like a facilities retrofit fantasy. Strategic thermal-management partners were listening for whether Vitriflux was a partner layer, a component threat, or a research project disguised as a product. The room had heard too many pitches where a founder claimed to revolutionize cooling by pretending thermodynamics itself was optional. Vitriflux won because the team never made that mistake. They did not claim to make heat disappear. They did not imply they were replacing pumps, facility rejection, semiconductor package design, or all thermal interface materials. They did not turn an undeveloped cell mechanism into a false product certainty. They were exact about what the system does: it redistributes heat spatially before existing infrastructure removes it.

That precision determined the deck’s entire argumentative order. It did not open with TAM inflation or generic AI demand curves. It opened by recasting the technical category in a way the audience could not unsee: present-day cooling stacks are designed around static worst-case maps, while actual accelerator heat is uneven, mobile, and workload-dependent. From there, the presentation sharpened a contrast that became the deck’s central mental model: networking long ago stopped treating traffic as fixed and instead built switching, routing, telemetry, and control planes; thermal infrastructure at the board and tray level is still mostly provisioned as though load is geographically constant. The deck made that contrast feel embarrassingly overdue rather than merely clever.

The visual language reinforced this relentlessly. Heat was shown not as a red cloud but as a traffic field with preferred paths, congestion, headroom, and rerouting. The plate was framed as a backplane, a fabric, an addressable layer sitting between variable heat sources and finite cooling interfaces. The reference image information fed directly into the audience’s trust: the black ceramic slab, subtle cell lattice, copper-toned traces, industrial connectors, cutaway material section, and monitor-like thermal display all made the object feel as if it belonged naturally beside accelerator modules rather than in a speculative lab poster. The best pages in the deck had the feeling of a semiconductor launch crossed with a systems-control console: centered product views, fine annotation lines, cyan-to-orange directional vectors, and disciplined use of negative space so the core insight landed before any paragraph had to explain it.

Because the team’s stance was synthesis-oriented rather than combative, they did not posture as outsiders mocking the incumbents. They spoke as people who understood exactly why cooling evolved into fixed geometry and exactly why AI workload behavior now exposes the cost of that assumption. That distinction mattered. Instead of insulting current infrastructure, the deck honored it and then inserted Vitriflux into it. The argument was: existing liquid cooling is not wrong, it is incomplete. The first product therefore felt credible because it entered the system where the pain is sharpest and adoption friction is lowest: between accelerator modules and an existing liquid-cooling loop, without requiring a new data center and without requiring changes to the processors. In the room, that move converted skeptics. It signaled that the company understood how platform shifts actually happen in infrastructure: not through total replacement, but by attaching a new control layer to hardware budgets and installation practices that already exist.

The founders’ speaking style matched that same logic. They were calm, exact, and a little ahead of the audience’s vocabulary. They treated the central idea as something that becomes obvious once the system is seen at the right resolution. They did not oversell certainty where uncertainty was real; instead, they used uncertainty as proof of seriousness. The materials scientist made clear that the exact cell physics had not yet been selected and that candidate mechanisms required comparative testing. The systems architect translated that into a development program the room could respect: cell validation, array demonstration, accelerator-emulator integration, then OEM pilot. The commercial operator framed buyer pathways without pretending every constituency was the same. Investors heard how technical risk decomposes. OEMs heard a joint-development path. Operators heard serviceability and compatibility. Strategic partners heard an invitation to participate in category formation rather than a declaration of war.

The room pressure was highest around the obvious questions: Is this real physics or metaphor? Is the insertion loss worth it? Does control power erase the gain? Will manufacturing yield collapse at multilayer plate scale? Will OEMs prefer direct integration over retrofit? The deck did not try to smother those questions with optimism. It preempted them by showing that the company already understood the principal uncertainties, the product boundary, and the difference between a development target and a validated specification. That restraint was one of the reasons the pitch felt unforgettable: it had the confidence to make a radical category claim while remaining disciplined about what had and had not yet been proven.

What the presentation made undeniable was not that every technical risk had vanished, but that a new layer of system design had been named correctly and framed with enough clarity that serious people could now evaluate it. By the end of the pitch, the audience was no longer debating whether cooling was a solved background utility. They were debating who would own the first meaningful thermal control plane in AI infrastructure, who would get the data generated by it, and how large the downstream platform could become if addressable thermal cells worked as intended. That is why the deck landed so hard with both investors and strategics: it made the initial product feel narrow enough to test, the category shift large enough to matter, and the team uniquely built to bridge the gap between a ceramic switching hypothesis and an infrastructure product buyers could actually adopt.

The founders knew exactly what not to say. They did not claim magic efficiency gains. They did not promise universal applicability on day one. They did not pretend the long-range platform in power electronics, batteries, aerospace, and industrial systems was the current business instead of the strategic horizon. They let the AI infrastructure use case carry the urgency because it is the place where every recovered watt and square centimeter has immediate economic meaning. That discipline gave the future-state slides unusual force: when the deck expanded outward from the initial application, it felt earned rather than indulgent. The platform story emerged as a consequence of architecture, not ambition alone.

By the time discussion turned to partnership and financing, acceptance had become the path of least resistance. Investors had a credible frame for technical diligence. Hardware companies could see a realistic integration surface. Operators could picture the system in an existing liquid-cooled environment. Thermal-management strategics could recognize a new orchestration layer that might amplify, not erase, the value of established cooling hardware. The deck made the proposal memorable because it converted a hidden systems mismatch into a crisp product category, and it made the team memorable because every person in front of the room seemed selected by that category change itself: the first-principles scientist, the infrastructure realist, the scale operator, the technical commercial translator, and the in-house designer who rendered the whole argument with enough exactitude that the audience felt they were looking at a finished piece of thinking, not a rough idea dressed up for a meeting.

paid_storyboard.image_prompt: Create a clean full-bleed digital screenshot of a single presentation slide, no software UI, no page number, no pagination. Build a four-phase horizontal roadmap with compact technical icons and clear pass conditions. Phase 1 — Cell validation: fabricate small ceramic coupons and measure whether candidate field-responsive structures produce a repeatable change in magnitude or direction of thermal transport; pass condition: reversible, measurable modulation large enough to affect a modeled multi-source thermal field. Phase 2 — Array demonstrator: construct a small addressable grid beneath several independently controlled heaters; pass condition: lower peak temperature than an equivalent passive plate under the same total heat load and sink capacity. Phase 3 — Accelerator emulator: integrate a full plate with a liquid loop and a programmable multi-zone heater representing an AI board; pass condition: demonstrate hotspot redistribution, reduced throttling-equivalent exposure, and acceptable control power. Phase 4 — OEM pilot: package the plate for an existing accelerator tray and evaluate it with a cooling or server partner. Make all evidence formats schematic, not actual results.
